source_doc: worldhistory.org Mystic Massacre of 1637; todayincthistory.com; pequotwar.org (Mashantucket Pequot Museum)
nations: Pequot (Mashantucket Pequot Tribal Nation; Eastern Pequot Tribal Nation)
place: Mistick Fort, Pequot Hill, Groton/Mystic CT; approx 41.37,-71.97 (APPROXIMATE, from Pequot Hill locality)
instrument: Treaty of Hartford, 1638-09-21 (colonial, English-Mohegan-Narragansett; Pequot not a consenting party)
summary: Connecticut and Massachusetts Bay forces under John Mason and John Underhill, with Mohegan and Narragansett allies, burned the fortified Pequot village at Mystic and killed those who fled. The 1638 Hartford treaty divided Pequot survivors and land among the victors and barred use of the Pequot name.
sources_cited_by_source: Mason and Underhill narratives (1637-38) per secondary sources
federal_account_contrast: Pre-US; outside Royce and Kappler entirely, so the atlas has no polygon for this taking.
map_implication: Add as colonial-era massacre point; tag eastern Connecticut Pequot homeland as taken by conquest, not cession. Battlefields of the Pequot War (ABPP-funded) has mapped the site; consult Mashantucket before display.
notes: Deaths 400 to 700 (secondary sources vary: 400-700, 500-700, 600-700, 'over 700'). English force about 77-90 plus 300 Native allies. Pequot survivors were enslaved, some shipped to the Caribbean (needs specific cite).

source_doc: Wikipedia 'Paxton Boys'; ICT News 'Ethnic cleansing in Pennsylvania'; Franklin, Narrative of the Late Massacres (1764, Miami U. PDF); digitalpaxton.org
nations: Susquehannock (Conestoga)

instrument: Conestoga Manor (Penn proprietary grant to Conestoga); no cession instrument located
summary: Paxton Boys (about 50 mounted settlers) killed 6 Conestoga at Conestoga Town, then on Dec 27 broke into the Lancaster workhouse and killed the 14 survivors held there for protection: 20 dead, the last of the community. No one was prosecuted.
federal_account_contrast: Pre-US; the land passed out of Conestoga hands by extermination, not by any treaty.
map_implication: Mark Conestoga Manor as land emptied by massacre; do not color as ceded. Land-disposition after 1763 NOT verified in this pass.
notes: Franklin says 57 men in first raid; others about 50. Sale of Conestoga Manor lands after the killings is an open question.

source_doc: Wikipedia 'Gnadenhutten massacre'; history.com; revolutionarywarjournal.com

instrument: Context: Treaty of Fort McIntosh 1785 (7 Stat. 16); Treaty of Greenville 1795 (7 Stat. 49)

notes: Deaths: 96 (commonly) to 'some 90'. 28 men, 29 women, 39 children often cited; verify. Atlas violations-seed-notes.csv already mentions Gnadenhutten.

source_doc: Atlas royce-entry-roles.csv (Royce 175, 226); Wikipedia 'Battle of Bad Axe'; Vernon Co. WI marker; globalsecurity.org
nations: Sauk; Meskwaki (Fox); Black Hawk's British Band; Ho-Chunk (Winnebago) context
place: Mouth of the Bad Axe River at the Mississippi, near Victory, Vernon Co WI; approx 43.48,-91.22 (APPROXIMATE)
instrument: Treaty of Fort Armstrong (Black Hawk Purchase), 1832-09-21
summary: US regulars, Illinois/Michigan Territory militia and the steamboat Warrior trapped Black Hawk's band, largely families, trying to cross the Mississippi; at least 150 were killed and others drowned or were killed by Dakota on the west bank. Seven weeks later the Sauk and Meskwaki ceded the Black Hawk Purchase strip in Iowa as the price of the war.
verbatim_quote: The confederated tribes of Sacs and Foxes cede to the U. S. all lands to which the said tribes have
sources_cited_by_source: Royce 1899 Schedule p.736 (as transcribed in atlas; 'ail' OCR corrected to 'all')

map_implication: Flag Royce 175 as signed after massacre (DURESS_MILITARY). Royce 226 (Keokuk reserve) was taken again 1836.
notes: Deaths: at least 150 (Wikipedia), about 300 (Vernon Co marker), 850 (globalsecurity, likely inflated). Ho-Chunk also ceded land at Fort Armstrong on 1832-09-15 (7 Stat. 370, from memory) in the same war settlement; not verified.

source_doc: Wikipedia 'Sacramento River massacre'; NAHC 'Timeline of Genocide Incidents in the Sacramento Valley Region' (nahc.ca.gov/cp/?p=2759, not fetched)

instrument: None ratified. California 1851-52 treaties unratified (Senate rejected 1852)

source_doc: Wikipedia 'Bloody Island massacre'; EBSCO Research Starter; Madley via secondary
nations: Pomo (Clear Lake / Eastern Pomo, Habematolel); Robinson Rancheria, Habematolel Pomo of Upper Lake descendants
place: Bo-no-po-ti (Bloody Island), north end of Clear Lake near Upper Lake, Lake Co CA; approx 39.15,-122.90 (APPROXIMATE; California Historical Landmark 427)

summary: US Army dragoons and infantry under Capt. Nathaniel Lyon and Lt. J.W. Davidson killed Pomo who had taken refuge on an island, in reprisal for the killing of Andrew Kelsey and Charles Stone, who had enslaved and starved Pomo laborers. The 1851 treaty for the area was never ratified.
federal_account_contrast: Royce treats the region as taken after the Senate rejected the 1851-52 treaties; the Army killing of Pomo a year earlier is invisible.

source_doc: Wikipedia 'Yontoket massacre'; nwgenocide.omeka.net (Cal Poly Humboldt) 'Yontocket Massacre (1853)'; NAHC Humboldt timeline; ndnhistoryresearch.com
nations: Tolowa Dee-ni' (Tolowa Dee-ni' Nation)
date: 1853 (late fall per NAHC; one historian argues summer solstice)
place: Yontocket (Yan'-daa-k'vt), Smith River, Del Norte Co CA; approx 41.93,-124.18 (APPROXIMATE)
instrument: None ratified; Tolowa included in no ratified treaty
summary: Settlers attacked Yontocket during the Nee-dash world-renewal ceremony, set the village afire, and shot people as they fled. The Tolowa center of the world was taken without any cession.
federal_account_contrast: No federal instrument; Royce at most shows later executive-order reservations.
map_implication: Mark Smith River Tolowa land NEVER_CEDED; point should carry Tolowa-preferred name; check with Tolowa Dee-ni' Nation on site display (ceremonial ground).

map_implication: Link point to Table Rock reserve polygon and to Siletz/Grand Ronde (Royce 407) with 'removal followed' edge.

source_doc: Wikipedia 'Mendocino War' and 'Walter S. Jarboe'; NAHC Mendocino timeline (summary); Baumgardner via Project MUSE excerpt; Madley
nations: Yuki (Ukomno'm); Round Valley Indian Tribes descendants; also Wailaki, Nomlaki, Pomo in region
place: Round Valley and Eel River country, Mendocino Co CA; approx 39.79,-123.24 (Round Valley/Covelo, APPROXIMATE regional centroid)
instrument: Nome Cult Farm / Round Valley Reservation (executive and statutory reservations, 1856 onward)
summary: With Gov. John Weller's permission, Walter Jarboe's Eel River Rangers raided Yuki communities for six months; Jarboe himself reported 283 'warriors' killed, not counting women and children, and the state paid the company. The Yuki were reduced to a few hundred and confined to Round Valley.
sources_cited_by_source: Jarboe report to Gov. Downey (via NAHC); California legislative claims
federal_account_contrast: Round Valley appears as a reservation granted to Indians; it was in fact a concentration of survivors of state-sponsored killing on their own land.

notes: Deaths: 283+ (Jarboe self-report), 'well over four hundred' (Baumgardner p.179). Payment: $11,143.43 (Wikipedia) vs 'over $9,000' (Baumgardner). Unresolved.

source_doc: Newsweek 2016 (citing Madley); Fullerton Observer (quoting Lindsay, Murder State); Wikiquote 'California genocide' (Madley quotation); California Government Code sec. 54260 (FindLaw snippet); calindian water study
nations: California Native nations statewide
place: California statewide; no single point
instrument: California militia appropriation and war-bond acts 1851-52 and later; federal reimbursement acts (Congress); Act for the Government and Protection of Indians 1850; 18 unratified 1851-52 treaties
summary: California financed about 24 militia campaigns against Native people between 1850 and 1861, spending roughly $1.29 to $1.5 million, and Congress reimbursed all but about $200,000. By Jan 1854 the state had already spent $924,259 on such expeditions; a later act appropriated up to $400,000 for nine campaigns of 1854-59 that killed at least 766 people.
sources_cited_by_source: Madley, An American Genocide (Yale UP 2016), ch. and appendices; Lindsay, Murder State (2012); Gov. Bigler message 1854
federal_account_contrast: Federal records frame these payments as reimbursing 'suppression of Indian hostilities'; scholars read them as federal funding of state killing campaigns that cleared unceded land.
map_implication: Create a statewide 'state-funded campaigns' layer keyed to NAHC atlas incident points; tag California land outside reservations NEVER_CEDED.
notes: Figures not reconciled: $1.29M (state code), $1.5M (Newsweek/Madley), $924,259 by 1854 (Lindsay/Bigler). Reimbursement act dates differ by source (1854, 1856, 1857 militia funding bill, 1860/1861 Act for payment of expenses... 1861 referenced by Smithsonian NMAI source explorer). A UC Press California History article ('The California Indian Scalp Bounty Myth') disputes popular bounty claims; keep claims tied to appropriations, not bounties. Statute cites need direct verification.

source_doc: MNHS Historic Fort Snelling 'US-Dakota War'; SD legislature resolutions; MPR News 2025; atlas royce-entry-roles.csv Royce 439, 440
nations: Dakota (Mdewakanton, Wahpekute, Sisseton, Wahpeton); Ho-Chunk (Winnebago) also removed
place: Lower Sioux Agency approx 44.53,-94.97; Fort Snelling camp approx 44.89,-93.18 (APPROXIMATE)
instrument: Act of Feb 16, 1863 (treaties declared void, annuities forfeited); Act of Mar 3, 1863 (removal of Sisseton, Wahpeton, Mdewakanton, Wahpekute); Act of Feb 21, 1863 (Winnebago)
instrument_cite: 12 Stat. 652; 12 Stat. 819; Act Feb 21 1863 (Winnebago) cite not checked
summary: After the 1862 war (begun amid withheld annuities), about 1,600 Dakota noncombatants were held in a stockade below Fort Snelling where 130 to 300 died; Congress then voided the Dakota treaties, forfeited annuities and land, and ordered removal from Minnesota. The Minnesota River reserve (Royce 440) was taken and sold.
verbatim_quote: The Minnesota River Sioux reserve of 1851 (kept south of the river by the 1858 treaties) was taken and ordered sold by the act of Mar. 3, 1863 after the 1862 outbreak.
sources_cited_by_source: Atlas plain-language Royce note (not a primary quote of Royce)
federal_account_contrast: Royce shows Royce 440 as 'ceded' 1863-03-03; it was confiscated by statute without Dakota consent. Ho-Chunk were removed though not party to the war.
map_implication: Recolor Royce 440 TAKEN_WITHOUT_CONSENT (statutory confiscation), Royce 439 likewise; add Fort Snelling camp point.
notes: Camp deaths: 160 officially recorded, 130-300 (MNopedia). South Dakota Senate passed repeal of removal act 2025 (32-3); final status not confirmed. Atlas violations-seed.csv already references Fort Snelling.

source_doc: Smithsonian Magazine 2024; Trust for Public Land; Deseret News; BLM blog 'Restoration at Wuda Ogwa'; KSL; Salt Lake Tribune

place: Boa Ogoi (Bear River at Beaver Creek), near Preston, Franklin Co ID; approx 42.10,-111.91 (APPROXIMATE; NHL boundary)

source_doc: NPS Sand Creek Massacre NHS place page and stories page; atlas violations-seed.csv V021; atlas royce-entry-roles.csv Royce 426, 477

place: Big Bend of the Marias River, MT; approx 48.4,-111.1 (APPROXIMATE, LOW confidence location; exact site not verified)
instrument: Executive order 1873-07-05 and Act of Apr 15, 1874 reducing Blackfeet reserve; Agreement 1888-05-01 (ratified 1888)

Eugene Baker's 2nd Cavalry attacked Heavy Runner's camp, which held papers of peace and was not the band sought; the Army counted 173 dead, mostly women, children and elders, and later accounts give 217 or more. Within four years the Blackfeet reservation was cut by executive order and statute without a treaty.
federal_account_contrast: Royce shows the 1873-74 reductions as administrative; the land cut came without consent shortly after the massacre.
map_implication: Flag Royce 565 reductions as TAKEN_WITHOUT_CONSENT, add massacre point once location verified.
notes: Causal link massacre -> 1873/74 reductions is temporal and contextual; do not state that one caused the other without a cite. Survivor breakdown 90 women, 50 children, 15 men (EJI).

nations: Aravaipa and Pinal Apache (San Carlos Apache Tribe descendants)

summary: A party of Tucson Anglo-Americans (William Oury), Mexican Americans (Jesus Maria Elias) and Tohono O'odham (Francisco Galerita) attacked Apache families living under Army protection, killing about 85 to 144, mostly women and children, and taking 27 to 30 or more children who were kept or sold. The Camp Grant reserve created afterwards was abolished in 1872.

source_doc: House Rpt 118-197 (resolution text); Senate Rpt 119-72; Spokesman-Review; New World Encyclopedia; atlas royce-entry-roles.csv Royce 699-705
nations: Mniconjou and Hunkpapa Lakota (Big Foot / Spotted Elk's band); Oglala Sioux Tribe, Cheyenne River Sioux Tribe descendants
place: Wounded Knee Creek, Pine Ridge Reservation SD; approx 43.14,-102.37
instrument: Act of Mar 2, 1889 (Sioux Agreement) dividing the Great Sioux Reservation; Act of Feb 28, 1877 (Black Hills)
summary: The 7th Cavalry killed about 250 to 375 Lakota, mostly women, children and elders, while disarming Spotted Elk's band. It came 21 months after the 1889 act broke up the Great Sioux Reservation and amid ration cuts.
federal_account_contrast: The Army awarded about 20 Medals of Honor; Royce shows the 1889 division as a reservation reorganization.

notes: Deaths: 153 killed + 150 missing (Army-style table), about 300 (Spokesman), 350-375 (congressional resolution). Medal of Honor count from memory.
